stories.headline: India can't fight its next war with 17 separate commands: Ex-Navy chief
stories.title: India can't fight its next war with 17 separate commands: Ex-Navy chief
stories.summary: Former COSC chairman backs theatre commands, and wants faster submarine building and highlights the need for three aircraft carriers.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: 's reluctance to divide its assets as the main obstacle.
"We cannot have 17 independent commands, none of them co-located," Lanba told TOI's Defence HQ podcast.
“The need of the hour is joint planning and joint execution." With AI shortening decision cycles, he said, separate services operating in separate environments is "not going to run".
A year before the 2019 attack, he said, he had the operations directorates of the three services draw up a joint plan for a "contingency short of war", which was passed down to all commands.
"That helped us when Pulwama happened, and finally it led to the Balakot incident," he said.
A theatre command, with one joint commander over Army, Navy and Air Force components, would be "much more effective".
The IAF's objections, Lanba said, "can all be worked out".
Strategic assets should stay with the Air Force, he argued, while tactical platforms such as attack helicopters should go to the Army.
"I know the Air Force guys will pan me for saying all this."
The Navy, about one-fourteenth the size of the Army, need not fear being subsumed, he said, since the maritime theatre would remain its own.
He would prefer two maritime theatres, one for each seaboard, but called the single one now proposed "fair enough".

article_sentences: Amid continuing face-offs with the Chinese Army along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) in Arunachal Pradesh since late July, the Indo-Tibetan Border.
Police (ITBP) has sanctioned the construction of new border infrastructure in the northeastern State, a senior government official told.
The Hindu.
Earlier, in February, the Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS) had cleared the third phase of the Indo-China Border Roads (ICBR-III) project.
Under the scheme, as many as 26 roads are to be constructed along the LAC in Arunachal Pradesh, another government official said.
The Union Government has not yet officially announced the ICBR-III project or publicly disclosed these details.
This is only the second time after the 2020 Galwan clashes in eastern Ladakh that a critical road infrastructure project has been sanctioned along the border with China.

The first phase of the ICBR was initiated in 2005 when it was decided that the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) would construct 27 priority roads with a total length of 608 km along the border with China.

The second phase of the ICBR, comprising 32 roads with a total length of 683 km, was approved on September 21, 2020, just months after 20 Indian soldiers were killed in violent clashes with the Chinese People’s Liberation Army in eastern Ladakh.

Since September, the ITBP has authorised the construction of 15 pedestrian suspension bridges and 18 log bridges in Upper Subansiri and Kurung Kumey districts, covering the areas bordering China in Arunachal Pradesh.
The project clearance came days after India hosted the 18th BRICS Summit from September 11 to 13 in New Delhi, which was attended by Chinese President Xi Jinping.

A government statement after the meeting said that Prime Minister Narendra Modi emphasised that peace and tranquillity in the border areas remains an essential basis for the continued development of bilateral relations.

stories.headline: Has the tide really turned for Indian markets?
stories.title: Has the tide really turned for Indian markets?
stories.summary: After navigating choppy waters for much of the year, Indian equities have staged a sharp recovery in less than a month. Once among Asia’s weakest-performing major markets, India is now regaining ground and gradually finding a balance. Both benchmark Indian indices, the Sensex and Nifty, gained nearly 12 percent each from October 15. Around the same time, the rupee has appreciated about 1.4 percent against the dollar.So, what has turned the tide? The turnaround began in mid-October, when strong corporate earnings, easing crude oil prices and a global rotation away from crowded AI trades sparked a rally in Indian equities. What began as a relief bounce has since developed into a broad-based market advance, supported by improving earnings visibility and the return of foreign institutional investors (FII).The rally stands out not only for its magnitude but also for its strength relative to other Asian markets. While several other Asian peers have remained subdued and technology-heavy markets have come under pressure from the unwinding of AI-linked positions, Indian equities have moved back within striking distance of their record highs.The shift reflects a change in investment strategy: As investors reassess richly valued AI trades and concerns over oil prices ease, capital is returning to markets that offer stronger earnings visibility. India, after trailing Asia for much of the year, is emerging as a key beneficiary of that rotation.Also Read: LTCG cut buzz turns spotlight on India's valuation premiumThe shift in investment sentiment towards India is finding validation by a few foreign brokerages. In November, Citi increased its target Nifty citing resilient earnings, softer crude prices and the prospect of capital rotating away from crowded AI trades.Surendra Goyal and Vijit Jain, analysts at Citi, feel multiple factors are working in favour of the Indian stock markets. These are decent earnings outlook, oil prices likely below prior fears, supporting macro stability and earnings, and more measured AI capex. “We raise our target multiple to 18 times (from 17) and roll forward to December 2027 (from September 27), resulting in a Nifty target of 28,000, implying a 12 percent upside,” they say.Meanwhile, HSBC has also upgraded India to overweight from neutral on improved valuations, corporate earnings and strong credit growth. “We upgrade India to overweight as we think it now offers resilient earnings and more reasonable valuations, and while high oil prices and El Niño remain risks, they are unlikely to materially weaken overall sentiment,” say analysts (Herald van der Linde, Prerna Garg and Adam Qi), HSBC.The HSBC analysts point out that the coming quarters could see modest downgrades if only energy prices remain elevated, but they don’t expect these to be significant enough to affect overall sentiment.As markets adopted a risk-off stance in October amid uncertainty surrounding the outcome of the US mid-term elections, prompting investors to pare their exposure to global equities, India stood out as FIIs returned.FIIs sold $2.2 billion worth of Indian equities in October, lower than the outflows recorded in the previous month. In contrast, domestic institutional investors (DIIs) invested $6.3 billion, extending their strong buying momentum for the 39th consecutive month.Also Read: Why investors may have to navigate volatility in the capital marketsAI trades: What ticks for India?The tide has also turned in India’s favour as investors question whether the AI investment boom has raced too far ahead of prospective returns, as an outcome of the US mid-term election results. In the US, Democrats won both chambers of Congress in a mid-term for the first time since 2006.The Democratic sweep in Texas triggered fears of data centre moratoriums and tighter regulation, driving a sharp repricing of AI infrastructure and build-out-dependent stocks. As a result, the Nasdaq (a technology-heavy index) fell, and the selloff spread beyond the US as SK Hynix and Samsung fell 23 percent and 18 percent respectively in November.The Korea index Kospi declined 13.6 percent (triggering a circuit breaker) while Taiwan’s Taiex slipped nearly 12 percent. Within Asia, capital rotated towards Chinese and Indian stocks, which have less exposure to AI hardware.“India offers diversification and low volatility in Asian markets dominated by AI stocks,” say analysts at HSBC.They explain that India’s investment case has become quite compelling relative to other markets. “In an environment where investors are seeking to diversify away from concentrated AI exposure, India stands out for its market depth, domestic demand orientation and relatively resilient macro backdrop,” they add.Analysts at HSBC elaborate that the market is becoming more receptive to resilient non-AI earnings stories. “India’s limited direct AI exposure, domestic demand, infrastructure investment and manufacturing expansion offer a differentiated backdrop and immunity from global volatility. Light foreign positioning and low volatility may also help,” they say.According to analysis by Goyal and Jain, over the past two years, AI has crowded out almost everything else. “If AI capex growth materially slows, it could have an impact on token availability/prices and, therefore, on the pace of AI-diffusion. However, focus on AI monetisation and outcomes should increase as Indian companies are relatively better placed there, in our view,” Goyal and Jain say.Also Read: Investing in a high-valuation market: What you need to knowForeign money and valuations gameValuations, previously a key concern, have moderated back towards historical averages, while corporate earnings have remained resilient despite the economy’s dependence on energy imports. At the same time, a pickup in domestic credit and sustained public sector capex should help keep growth stable, say analysts.Foreign investors sold about $30.4 billion of Indian equities in 2026 so far but are relooking at India with a fresh lens since mid-October as their buying of Indian stocks has picked up pace. “A correction in AI-linked assets, which has hit Korea and Taiwan hardest, could redirect emerging market flows towards India,” says Apoorva Javadekar, chief economist, Shriram Research.Improvement in FII sentiment and easing geopolitical challenges could help offset the headwinds that have weighed on Indian markets over the past two years and lay the foundation for a sustained market rally.“Given India's healthy macroeconomic fundamentals, strong corporate earnings, a meaningful correction in valuations from their 2024 peak levels, and robust domestic liquidity, any moderation in the global AI trade could encourage a stronger and more sustained revival in FII interest in relatively underperforming emerging markets such as India,” says Deven Mistry, analyst at Motilal Oswal Financial Services.As per MSCI, there are $1.5 trillion assets benchmarked to MSCI EM. Assuming 20 percent, every 100 basis points increase in active weight could result in inflows of $12 billion, suggests analysis by Goyal and Jain. India’s weightage in MSCI EM is close to multi-year lows currently.They add that lower oil price could help India’s macro and earnings assumptions. A $10 lower oil price would help current account deficit by 30 to 40bps and inflation by 50 bps.

opening: After navigating choppy waters for much of the year, Indian equities have staged a sharp recovery in less than a month.
Once among Asia’s weakest-performing major markets, India is now regaining ground and gradually finding a balance.
body: Both benchmark Indian indices, the Sensex and Nifty, gained nearly 12 percent each from October 15.
Around the same time, the rupee has appreciated about 1.4 percent against the dollar.
So, what has turned the tide?
The turnaround began in mid-October, when strong corporate earnings, easing crude oil prices and a global rotation away from crowded AI trades sparked a rally in Indian equities.
What began as a relief bounce has since developed into a broad-based market advance, supported by improving earnings visibility and the return of foreign institutional investors (FII).
The rally stands out not only for its magnitude but also for its strength relative to other Asian markets.

While several other Asian peers have remained subdued and technology-heavy markets have come under pressure from the unwinding of AI-linked positions, Indian equities have moved back within striking distance of their record highs.

The shift reflects a change in investment strategy: As investors reassess richly valued AI trades and concerns over oil prices ease, capital is returning to markets that offer stronger earnings visibility.
India, after trailing Asia for much of the year, is emerging as a key beneficiary of that rotation.
The shift in investment sentiment towards India is finding validation by a few foreign brokerages.
In November, Citi increased its target Nifty citing resilient earnings, softer crude prices and the prospect of capital rotating away from crowded AI trades.
These are decent earnings outlook, oil prices likely below prior fears, supporting macro stability and earnings, and more measured AI capex.
“We raise our target multiple to 18 times (from 17) and roll forward to December 2027 (from September 27), resulting in a Nifty target of 28,000, implying a 12 percent upside,” they say.
Meanwhile, HSBC has also upgraded India to overweight from neutral on improved valuations, corporate earnings and strong credit growth.

“We upgrade India to overweight as we think it now offers resilient earnings and more reasonable valuations, and while high oil prices and El Niño remain risks, they are unlikely to materially weaken overall sentiment,” say analysts (Herald van der Linde, Prerna Garg and Adam Qi), HSBC.

The HSBC analysts point out that the coming quarters could see modest downgrades if only energy prices remain elevated, but they don’t expect these to be significant enough to affect overall sentiment.

As markets adopted a risk-off stance in October amid uncertainty surrounding the outcome of the US mid-term elections, prompting investors to pare their exposure to global equities, India stood out as FIIs returned.
FIIs sold $2.2 billion worth of Indian equities in October, lower than the outflows recorded in the previous month.
In the US, Democrats won both chambers of Congress in a mid-term for the first time since 2006.
The Democratic sweep in Texas triggered fears of data centre moratoriums and tighter regulation, driving a sharp repricing of AI infrastructure and build-out-dependent stocks.
As a result, the Nasdaq (a technology-heavy index) fell, and the selloff spread beyond the US as SK Hynix and Samsung fell 23 percent and 18 percent respectively in November.
Within Asia, capital rotated towards Chinese and Indian stocks, which have less exposure to AI hardware.
“India offers diversification and low volatility in Asian markets dominated by AI stocks,” say analysts at HSBC.
They explain that India’s investment case has become quite compelling relative to other markets.

“In an environment where investors are seeking to diversify away from concentrated AI exposure, India stands out for its market depth, domestic demand orientation and relatively resilient macro backdrop,” they add.
Analysts at HSBC elaborate that the market is becoming more receptive to resilient non-AI earnings stories.
“India’s limited direct AI exposure, domestic demand, infrastructure investment and manufacturing expansion offer a differentiated backdrop and immunity from global volatility.
Light foreign positioning and low volatility may also help,” they say.
According to analysis by Goyal and Jain, over the past two years, AI has crowded out almost everything else.
“If AI capex growth materially slows, it could have an impact on token availability/prices and, therefore, on the pace of AI-diffusion.
However, focus on AI monetisation and outcomes should increase as Indian companies are relatively better placed there, in our view,” Goyal and Jain say.

Foreign money and valuations gameValuations, previously a key concern, have moderated back towards historical averages, while corporate earnings have remained resilient despite the economy’s dependence on energy imports.
At the same time, a pickup in domestic credit and sustained public sector capex should help keep growth stable, say analysts.
“A correction in AI-linked assets, which has hit Korea and Taiwan hardest, could redirect emerging market flows towards India,” says Apoorva Javadekar, chief economist, Shriram Research.

Improvement in FII sentiment and easing geopolitical challenges could help offset the headwinds that have weighed on Indian markets over the past two years and lay the foundation for a sustained market rally.

“Given India's healthy macroeconomic fundamentals, strong corporate earnings, a meaningful correction in valuations from their 2024 peak levels, and robust domestic liquidity, any moderation in the global AI trade could encourage a stronger and more sustained revival in FII interest in relatively underperforming emerging markets such as India,” says Deven Mistry, analyst at Motilal Oswal Financial Services.
As per MSCI, there are $1.5 trillion assets benchmarked to MSCI EM.
India’s weightage in MSCI EM is close to multi-year lows currently.
They add that lower oil price could help India’s macro and earnings assumptions.
A $10 lower oil price would help current account deficit by 30 to 40bps and inflation by 50 bps.

stories.headline: RBI rate hike in December: SBI now expects just 25 bps despite inflation crossing 6%
stories.title: RBI rate hike in December: SBI now expects just 25 bps despite inflation crossing 6%
stories.summary: In its latest Ecowrap report dated November 12, SBI Research said the balance of probabilities had shifted decisively towards a smaller rate increase at the Reserve Bank of India's December Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'monetary policy' in summary weight 24
article_sentences: The revision comes after India's consumer price index (CPI) inflation climbed to a two-year high of 6.09% in October, exceeding the RBI's upper tolerance limit for the first time under the new CPI series.
“When facts change, I change my mind.
What do you do sir?” the SBI Research report stated, as it revised its December rate hike forecast from 50 basis points to 25 basis points.

Earlier, the research team had outlined two possibilities: an aggressive 50-bps hike or a 25-bps repo rate increase accompanied by another 25-bps tightening through widening the interest rate corridor.
However, recent domestic and international developments have strengthened the case for a more measured response.
SBI identified four developments behind its revised forecast.
First, the RBI's efforts to stabilise the rupee and ease liquidity pressures have yielded results.
The currency recovered below ₹94 against the dollar before weakening again, while overnight money market rates moderated.
Second, improving foreign capital flows could reduce pressure on the currency.
SBI noted foreign institutional investment inflows of approximately $7.68 billion since November 4, alongside a 0.7% appreciation in the rupee.
Third, easing geopolitical tensions have improved the crude oil outlook.
Brent crude prices have declined approximately 11% following the US elections, potentially reducing India's imported inflation pressures.

stories.title: India's retail inflation crosses RBI's upper limit of 6 per cent in October
stories.summary: Overall food inflation in October stood at 8.94 per cent as the prices of onions shot up by 116.22 per cent while garlic turned costlier by 60.74 per cent.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Overall food inflation in October stood at 8.94 per cent as the prices of onions shot up by 116.22 per cent while garlic turned costlier by 60.74 per cent.

New Delhi: India's retail inflation, based on the new Consumer Price Index (CPI) series, rose to 6.09 per cent in October this year compared to the same month of the previous year to cross the RBI's upper limit for the first time after two years, according to data released by the Ministry of Statistics on Thursday.
Ginger and lemon prices also rose by 48.32 per cent and 47.30 per cent, respectively, during the month.

On the other hand, potato prices fell by 14.24 per cent during the month, while cauliflower and coconut turned cheaper by 10.57 per cent and 5.6 per cent, respectively, in October compared to the same month of the previous year.
Silver jewellery was among the commodities that posted the highest inflation during the month, with prices surging as much as 52.39 per cent.
The CPI inflation has breached the upper limit of the RBI safe zone, raising expectations of a rate hike by the RBI in the next monetary policy review.
The tolerance zone of the RBI ranges from 2 per cent to 6 per cent.
The RBI's monetary policy aims to keep inflation within this zone as it balances its objective of promoting economic growth with stability.
The monetary policy committee voted unanimously to increase the policy repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.5 per cent on October 7.
Acceleration of inflation in key economies has prompted a shift towards hawkish monetary policy.
The US Fed hiked by 25 bps in September.
RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra said in the monetary policy statement on October 7 that CPI inflation increased to 4.8 per cent in August 2026 from 4.5 per cent in July.

stories.headline: Cabinet approves ₹62,370-crore fertiliser subsidy for Rabi season
stories.title: Cabinet approves ₹62,370-crore fertiliser subsidy for Rabi season
stories.summary: The package includes Nutrient Based Subsidy (NBS) rates for phosphatic and potassic (P&K) fertilisers for the period October 1, 2026, to March 31, 2027.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'cabinet approves' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Union Cabinet on Wednesday approved a fertiliser subsidy package of Rs 62,370 crore for the Rabi 2026-27 season, a 64 per cent increase over the Rs 37,952 crore allocated for the previous Rabi season, with provisions to keep Di-ammonium Phosphate (DAP) available to farmers at a fixed price of Rs 1,350 per bag.
The package includes Nutrient Based Subsidy (NBS) rates for phosphatic and potassic (P&K) fertilisers for the period October 1, 2026, to March 31, 2027.

It also provides for special assistance for DAP, extension of these provisions to Triple Superphosphate (TSP) and Monoammonium Phosphate (MAP), freight subsidy for Single Superphosphate (SSP), and continuation of subsidy on ammonium sulphate.
The enhanced outlay comes against the backdrop of global fertiliser price volatility and disruptions arising from the West Asia crisis.
The government said the package would ensure adequate availability of fertilisers during the Rabi season, while keeping input costs stable for farmers.
Under the approved NBS rates, the subsidy has been fixed at Rs 94.21 per kg for nitrogen, Rs 66.11 per kg for phosphorus, Rs 2.38 per kg for potash and Rs 10.42 per kg for sulphur.
The government will continue special provisions beyond the NBS framework to ensure DAP is available at Rs 1,350 per bag.
These provisions have also been extended to imported and domestic TSP and imported MAP.
The freight subsidy on SSP will continue during the Rabi season to encourage its use as an affordable alternative to DAP.
The subsidy on imported and domestic ammonium sulphate will also be continued.
In a push to strengthen domestic production and reduce import dependence, the Cabinet has also approved a sulphur package for domestic manufacturers.
Under this, manufacturers will receive 20 per cent of the actual procurement cost of sulphur, subject to a floor price of $800 per tonne.

article_sentences: The Secretary to Government, Department of Personnel and Training, has informed the Madras High Court that the Central Government has accorded sanction to prosecute two IAS officers in connection with the tender irregularities scam.
When the matter came up for hearing, Justice Anand Venkatesh was informed that the Centre had accorded sanction to prosecute the two officers – KS Kandasamy and K Vijaya Karthikeyan.
The court was also informed that the investigating agency would be acting upon the sanction and take steps to conduct an investigation against the officers and file a final report.

Taking note of the sanction, the judge orally remarked that the present case was a classic example of how the criminal law worked in the country where the law moved fast against the poor but needed a push when the case related to influential people.
“Classic case of how criminal law works in this country.
See how much effort has been put in by so many people.
Things move fast for poor people.
But for influential people, we have to push and push, and ultimately we are here,” the court orally remarked.
The court was hearing a contempt petition filed by NGO Arappor Ayakkam against the delay in proceedings against former Minister SP Velumani and three IAS officers in a tender irregularities case.
SP Velumani is accused of abusing his official position while he was serving as the Minister for Municipal Administration.
It is alleged that he had extended large-scale favouritism while awarding tenders for road works in Chennai Corporation and Coimbatore Municipal Corporation to his relatives and his close associates.
Arappor Iyakkam, an NGO, made a complaint with the DVAC.

stories.headline: India's Ambekar Meetei scripts history with boxing gold at Dakar Youth Olympics
stories.title: India's Ambekar Meetei scripts history with boxing gold at Dakar Youth Olympics
stories.summary: Lairenlakpam Ambekar Meetei made history at Dakar 2026 by clinching the gold medal in the men's 50kg boxing category, edging out Ireland’s Kristian Jubani in a nail-biting 3-2 final. His path to glory included a resounding 5-0 victory over Colombia's Izzon Jeffrey Galea Arevalo. This achievement signifies a significant moment for Indian sports, breaking a 16-year streak without an Indian boxer in the finals of the Youth Olympic Games.

Mahesh Bhagwat has been appointed Hyderabad Police Commissioner, while V C Sajjanar will head Telangana Fire, Disaster Response and Civil Defence.
